summary:
Annabelle (INT015) is a 78-year-old artist displaced by the Eaton Fire whose home—including a front rental unit and her art studio—was completely destroyed. The fire severed her primary income stream, placing her on mortgage forbearance while paying significantly higher rent, and left her navigating overlapping SBA loans, disaster unemployment, and insurance paperwork under a brain fog she describes as markedly worse since the fire. She entered the post-fire period in profound shock, preferring not to speak at all, and moved through her car, a friend's house, and ultimately a Pasadena apartment. A persistent longing for home—not merely the structure but the stability and identity it anchored—runs throughout the interview, alongside heightened intrusive imagery of disasters. She anticipates a depressive episode when she eventually catalogs her lost artwork for the insurance inventory, a task she has been deferring.

Despite cognitive difficulties, Annabelle is a practiced ChatGPT user who turns to it before Google for practical questions and attempted to use it to reconstruct Amazon purchase records for her lost-belongings claim. Her street WhatsApp group and block captain have been crucial information hubs. Her primary stated need at the one-year mark is financial clarity; she describes feeling out on the street again after building a comfortable independent life, and is actively seeking a bookkeeper to organize her funds.

Her reaction to the TAC MVP demo was pointed. When the bot responded to a practical task request with an invitation to relax, she pushed back emphatically, articulating that she wants AI to execute tasks rather than infer emotional needs. She characterizes AI as a logistics tool, not a therapeutic companion, and explicitly stated she does not see it as an emotional support person. She also raised direct data-privacy concerns about who controls AI systems and whether they share user information. No specific feature endorsements emerged during the demo session. Annabelle agreed to give feedback on a future version.

Socially, she describes an unexpected openness to people that deepened since the fire, though loneliness remains a daily management challenge. She has lost some friendships due to reduced capacity for phone conversations and is now managing a close friend entering dementia—an added caregiving burden on top of her own recovery. Her deepest conviction about emotional recovery is that it requires physical human presence in a group setting.
